content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a multi-modal prompt learning method called MaPLe for CLIP to adapt to downstream tasks. The authors argue that uni-modal (either text or vision) prompting for CLIP is sub-optimal and multi-modal prompting is essential to dynamically adapt both the text and vision feature space to the downstream task. MaPLe adopts deep prompting which learns prompts for every layer of the text and the image encoder in CLIP with a coupling function between the text and the vision prompts to induce mutual synergies between the two modalities. Experiments on three types of representative tasks, namely, generalization to novel classes, new target datasets and unseen domain shifts show improvement over previous state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:

- The paper is well written and structured with nice diagrams.
- The design choices for the proposed approach are well motivated.

**Weaknesses**:

- The technical novelty of the paper is very limited. It simply combines several existing techniques like deep prompting, language prompting, and vision prompting for developing a technique for adapting CLIP to downstream tasks. The motivation behind multimodal prompting is not clear. Why one should do multimodal prompting or why it outperforms unimodal prompts should be clearly discussed in the paper. Is there any relation between the nature of downstream tasks and the type of prompt learning? On what type of classes, multimodal prompting is preferred? A through analysis on this should be included in the paper to justify the motivation of multimodal prompt learning for vision-language models.

- The basic objective of any prompt learning is approach is to enable parameter efficient adaptation of large language models to several downstream tasks. One of the major aspects of comparison which is missing across the experiments is the number of learnable parameters for various approaches. This is essential because the number of parameters learnt improves the performance, which makes comparing approaches with similar numbers of parameters essential.  Specifically, Co-CoOp has in total around 41K parameters, but a single use of the coupling function F adds 512x768 ~ 393K parameters, which is a lot! A through comparison on number of learnable parameters of MaPLe with other methods should be included in the paper to demonstrate the accuracy vs number of parameters in adaptation of CLIP.

- Another major issue of this paper is on unfair comparison between the baselines. E.g., in Table 1, MaPLe compares with CoCoOp and shows improvement but this improvement is mainly due to the deep prompting. A fair comparison would be to compare CoCoOp without using deep prompting. It is very well known that deep prompting improves the performance of any prompt learning method as it increases the number of tunable parameters. Similarly, in Table 3, comparison with CoOp is not fair. Without a fair comparison, it is very hard to see the effectiveness of the proposed method over existing methods. Although supplementary material shows a comparison with CoCoOp by increasing the number of parameters, it would be fair to have a non-deep version of MaPLe (basically J=1) with Co-CoOp and CoOp. As can be seen from Figure-4 (left), J=1 provides a performance lower than 75%. Moreover, it is not clear how the authors modified CoCoOp to obtain “heavier Co-CoOp”? The deep prompting version of CoCoOp should add prompts at intermediate layers instead simply increasing the number of parameters in the meta network.

- Beside ViT-B/16 CLIP, experiments should be done on another CLIP variant or other vision-language models like DeCLIP, FILIP, CLOOB, CyCLIP. Since the approach is agnostic to the architecture and models, I would encourage the authors to perform additional experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on other vision-language models.

- It is mentioned that “a photo of a <category>” is used to initialize the prompt before training, but the number of learnable tokens in the prompt is 2. How was the initialization done?

- The difference between “CoOp” and “CoOp in Co-CoOp setting” is not clear in Table-3.

- In Figure-4, are all the variants trained for the same number of epochs? In the line just above Figure-4 as well as in the caption, there is a mention of a “held-out validation set”, can the authors elaborate on how the validation set was chosen? Does it contain additional label data other than the few-shot data used for training?

- As mentioned in Table-6 of Supplemental Material, the hyperparameters used for the approaches mentioned in Table-1 are different. It would be good to see the results for all the approaches with the same hyperparameters as used for MaPLe.

- Besides generalization experiments, what about comparison with CoOp on the standard closed-set few-shot image classification setting used in the CoOp paper (using same number of parameters)? What components of the proposed approach makes it suitable for improved generalization? 

- In Figure-5, how is the diversity of a dataset measured?

- In the implementation details, what is d_{vl}?

- Minor typo: in the last line of section-4.2 - “Fruther” → “Further”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of the problem statement is clear. The authors have provided proper justification for various design choices in the approach like the coupling function and have explained their role clearly. Authors have provided the source code, which make the work reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although this paper is well-written, I’d like to rate the current submission as a clear rejection due to lack of convincing experiments. This paper combines existing approaches and applies this combination for prompting CLIP without a fair comparison with existing methods. In particular, prompt learning was introduced to efficiently adapt large models to downstream tasks by only tuning as less parameters as possible, making parameter analysis of MaPLe very crucial, which is missing and majorly shapes my decision. I highly recommend authors to update the paper with full revision and adding thorough experiments.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides a framework capable of Multi-modal Prompt Learning (MaPLe) via vision-language prompts. Specifically, MaPLe tunes both pre-trained vision and language models through the learnable context prompts, and keep the rest parts of the models frozen. The vision prompts are conditioned on language prompts via a V-L coupling function F that can induce mutual synergy between the two modalities.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Generally, the paper is well-written and the code is available. However, some points still needs to be clarified:
- Any other connecting methods between vision and text prompts are considered (for example, joint learning)?
- For the coupling function, have you experimented with other functions besides the linear layer? If so, what is its performance?
- For cross-dataset evaluation, do you train it on ImageNet and directly test it on the other dataset without any training/ tuning of the - -prompts? If so, what is the purpose of using prompts here? I asked this question because the purpose of prompt learning is to adapt the model based on the target data, if the prompt is not adjusted when data changes, what are the extra benefits prompts can bring, compared to a set of additional parameters in a frozen model?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper shows the effectiveness of prompting for both vision and language branched to adapt the large-scale pertained V-L models. The method shows improved performance on generalization from base-to-novel classes, cross-dataset generalization, and domain generalization, compared with the established Co-CoOp method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea to adapt both the vision and language part of the model with prompt learning is interesting.
2. The empirical results show the effectiveness of the proposed method on base-to-novel class generalization, cross-dataset generalization, and domain generalization, and compared with CoCoOp which is one the latest methods.
3. Ablation study in Table 1 shows the importance of the proposed coupling function between multiple domains.

Weakness:
1. The paper should compare finetuning the whole backbone with an optimal learning rate obtained from grid search, say learning rate from 1e-8 to 1e-3. As far as the reviewer knows, fine-tuning can be a very competitive method with a carefully tuned learning rate. Does the gain solely come from using a deep prompt with more parameters, or due to the multimodal design? If due to more parameters, fine-tuning can be a stronger way to improve.
2. Question: why does training prompt on one dataset enable generation to novel tasks and categories instead of overfitting only to the ones that the model has been trained on? For example, [1] shows that directly training the model one distribution reduces the performance on distribution shifts.

[1] Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models. Wortsman et al.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written, with good quality.

The method is novel.

Code is provided yet not containing the algorithm.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a novel method for prompting the V-L model, and show improved performance. Overall I recommend for acceptance.

content.title: MaPLe: Multi-modal Prompt Learning
content.TL;DR: Multi-modal prompt learning for improving synergy between learned language and vision representations for fine-tuning CLIP on downstream image recognition tasks.
content.abstract: Pre-trained vision-language (V-L) models such as CLIP have shown excellent generalization ability to downstream tasks. However, they are sensitive to the choice of input text prompts and require careful selection of prompt templates to perform well. Inspired by the Natural Language Processing (NLP) literature, recent CLIP adaptation approaches learn prompts as the textual inputs to fine-tune CLIP for downstream tasks. We note that using prompting to adapt representations in a single branch of CLIP (language or vision) is sub-optimal since it does not allow the flexibility to dynamically adjust both representation spaces on a downstream task. In this work, we propose Multi-modal Prompt Learning (MaPLe) for both vision and language branches to improve alignment between the vision and language representations. Our design promotes strong coupling between the vision-language prompts to ensure mutual synergy and discourages learning independent uni-modal solutions. Further, we learn separate prompts across different early stages to progressively model the stage-wise feature relationships to allow rich context learning. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on three representative tasks of generalization to novel classes, new target datasets and unseen domain shifts. Compared with the state-of-the-art method Co-CoOp, MaPLe exhibits favorable performance and achieves an absolute gain of 3.45% on novel classes and 2.72% on overall harmonic-mean, averaged over 11 diverse image recognition datasets. Our code and models will be publicly released.
